activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur.
story:
The community hall smelled like cardamom and fried dough, and Brooke's little cousin Raj would not stop pulling her sleeve. Outside, the nagar kirtan was lining up, and Brooke wanted to figure something out before it started. She had noticed that five people in saffron robes always walked at the very front, and she wanted to know if it was the same five every year or just whoever showed up.

She tested it by asking to see the program sheet, but the front page only tried to summarize the whole day in one paragraph: prayers at ten, procession at eleven, lunch at noon. No names. So she tried something else. She counted the people in saffron and memorized their faces, the tall man with the gray beard, the woman with the blue turban, three others. If the same five led again next Vaisakhi, it was a job. If it changed, it was a sign-up sheet.

Raj tugged harder. "Why does today matter so much?" he asked Uncle Harpreet, who was adjusting a flag pole with a buoyant orange pennant snapping above it.

"Sikhs celebrate Vaisakhi as the day in 1699 when Guru Gobind Singh, the tenth Sikh Guru, founded the Khalsa at Anandpur," Uncle said, then went back to the pole.

Brooke stood still. Khalsa. Founded at Anandpur. She counted the five in saffron again, and this time the pattern had a shape: five leaders, like five fingers on a hand. She did not know the whole story yet, but she knew what to watch for.

"Raj," she said, "walk with me to the front." She took his hand and pulled him through the crowd, past the drummers, until they stood at the edge of the road where the five would pass. She pointed at the tall man with the gray beard.

"Count them," she said. "Five. Watch what they do first."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The first Super Bowl was played on January 15, 1967, and the Green Bay Packers beat the Kansas City Chiefs 35 to 10.
story:
Grandpa Ray claimed he remembered the very first Super Bowl, and Luke wanted to catch him in a mistake. "I watched it in my dorm room," Grandpa said from the recliner, loud enough to be heard over the game. "Best day of my young life."

"Who played?" Luke asked. He had his notebook on his knee, but he kept his pencil still.

"The Packers and the Chiefs."

"What was the score?"

"Thirty-five to ten," Grandpa said. "Packers."

The living room was packed, five uncles and two neighbors, all watching the current game on the big television. Every chair was taken, and Luke sat on the floor between the coffee table and the couch. The plan formed quietly in his head. If Grandpa had watched the game in a dorm room, he had been in college, so he could not have been too young. Luke could test this without asking the year directly, because asking would give the whole trick away.

"You lived in a dorm your first year of college, right?" Luke said.

"Second floor, Henderson Hall," Grandpa said.

"And you still have your college mug. The one from graduation." Luke had seen it on the shelf a hundred times, gold letters on blue ceramic. Grandpa pulled it down and set it on the table, pleased to show off. Luke read the numbers out loud. Then he counted on his fingers, starting from that graduation year and going back to see whether a college freshman could have been watching television in 1967, when the first Super Bowl was played on January 15. He simulated the timeline in his head, year by year, and each step matched. Grandpa had been in a dorm, of a college age, on that exact date. There was no hole in the story.

"You're checking up on me," Grandpa said, but he was grinning.

"I was being pessimistic," Luke admitted. "I thought you made up the score."

"Why would I make up thirty-five to ten?"

Uncle Marty laughed from the couch. "Because you make up your fishing stories."

"Resentment," Grandpa said, pointing at Marty. "That's pure resentment, from a man who's never out-fished me."

"Show me the notebook," Marty said to Luke, so Luke turned it around. He had written the date, the teams, and the score, each line checked off. On the television the teams ran one more play, and the whole room leaned forward at the same time.

"Watch the game," Grandpa said. "Someday I'll tell you I remember this one too."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: A swimmer caught in a rip current can usually escape by swimming parallel to the beach, out of the narrow current, rather than straight against it.
story:
Emma's aunt had a house two blocks from the ocean, and the whole first morning of the trip, Emma's little cousin Theo wanted nothing but the beach. He ran ahead on the wooden walkway, dragging a boogie board with a cracked, brittle spine of plastic down the middle, while Emma carried the towels and tried to categorize the clouds overhead, sorting the flat gray ones from the puffy white ones, because the gray ones meant rain and rain meant going home early.

At the top of the beach steps a sign stood in the sand. RIP CURRENTS it said, in red letters, and under that: IF CAUGHT, SWIM PARALLEL TO THE BEACH. Theo read it slowly, frowning. "Parallel? What does that mean? Like sideways?"

"Sort of," Emma said. "Along the shore, instead of back toward it." She traced two lines in the sand with her toe, one for the beach and one for the swimmer moving alongside it.

They swam near the lifeguard stand for an hour. Then Theo paddled out after a wave and Emma, watching, noticed something wrong. He wasn't getting closer to shore no matter how hard he kicked. He was stuck in the same spot, drifting sideways, and his face had gone from playing to scared.

Emma remembered the sign and the two lines in the sand. Don't swim at it, she told herself. Swim along it. "Theo!" she shouted, cupping her hands. "Don't swim toward me! Swim that way, down the beach!" She pointed hard to her left, along the shore, and he turned, his arms cutting sideways through the water. Slowly, then all at once, he was moving again, and a small wave carried him in until he could stand, gasping and dripping, in front of her.

"You okay?" she asked, kneeling and putting a towel around his shoulders.

"I couldn't get back," he whispered. "The water kept pulling."

"I know. But you went sideways and it let you go." She squeezed his shoulder and walked him up to the dry sand, where she dug two fresh lines side by side and said, "Want me to show you again?"

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: Ted Williams batted .406 in 1941 and is the last Major League Baseball player to finish a season above .400.
story:
Andrew's name sat fourteenth on the league scoring list, and he had counted the names twice before practice ended. Fourteen sounded terrible. He had eleven points in nine games, and he knew that if he had scored on that breakaway last Saturday he would have been at twelve, which might have moved him up two spots. One number held his whole season, and he did not like how small it was.

Grandpa Ray was waiting by the doors with two hot chocolates, steam rising past the transparent panels of glass where the zamboni was still smoothing the ice. "You look like a kid doing math homework in his head," Grandpa said.

"They post the rankings online," Andrew said. "I'm fourteenth." He kept his voice low because Kowalski, who was third on the list, was lacing up his skates ten feet away.

Grandpa sipped his chocolate. "You know what I like about hockey? The numbers lie a little, and they tell the truth a little. One guy gets points because his line thrives on passing. Another guy gets nothing because his team is a mess. The list can't show you that." He set the cup down on the rail. "Tell you what. I'll make a bet with you. Baseball, since you like to argue about it. I bet nobody has hit four hundred in a whole season since before I was born."

Andrew frowned. "Nobody? Everyone hits .300 sometimes." He pulled out his phone, thumbs cold, and searched for highest batting average seasons. The list loaded under the rink's flickering wifi. Ted Williams, 1941, .406. He scrolled down past Williams looking for a later one. There were seasons of .390 and .384, close calls and heartbreaks, but nothing after 1941 crossed .400. He scrolled all the way to the bottom of the list of the greats, and every single one of them had either retired or been dead for decades before Andrew was born.

"Ted Williams," Andrew said slowly. "He batted .406 in 1941. And he's the last one. The last Major League player to finish a season above .400." He looked up. "That's before you were born?"

"Nineteen fifty-two, that's me," Grandpa said. "So pay up."

Andrew slid him the second hot chocolate, which Grandpa had bought for him anyway. On the screen behind them, the sports ticker ran a news item about a new tariff on imported gear, and Kowalski's dad groaned and said new sticks would cost a fortune by spring. Andrew barely heard him. He was still scrolling, looking at .406, thinking that Williams must have failed six times out of ten, more than half the time, and was still the best anyone had done in his grandfather's whole lifetime. Fourteenth place suddenly felt like a very small number that held a very large game.

He walked back toward the ice with his stick over his shoulder. "Hey, Kowalski," he called. "You want to work on the give-and-go? I need about two hundred more assists to catch Ted Williams."

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: The crowd 'wave' became known worldwide at the 1986 FIFA World Cup in Mexico, so many English speakers outside North America call it the Mexican wave.
story:
Carson squeezed onto the couch between his dad and Mr. Okafor just as the referee blew the whistle for the second half. The whole living room had been calibrating all afternoon, moving snacks and chairs until everyone at Mr. Okafor's house could see the television, and now twelve people leaned forward at once. The score was tied, and there were only twenty minutes left.

When the home team nearly scored, the whole crowd in the stadium stood up section by section, arms rising around the bowl like water moving through a channel. "Look at that Mexican wave," said Priya, Mr. Okafor's cousin, who was visiting from London for the month.

"A what wave?" Carson asked.

"The Mexican wave," Priya said. "Everyone at home calls it that."

Carson frowned. Everyone he knew just called it the wave. He thought about last summer, when he had insisted on naming the fort in the woods after himself and his friend Jonah had stopped coming for two whole weeks. Names felt small until they weren't. Maybe the wave had a different name in different places, the way soda and pop did, and maybe Priya's name had a reason behind it that he couldn't see directly. He decided to test it.

"Priya, when did people start calling it the Mexican wave?" He kept his voice low so his dad wouldn't shush him.

"1986," she whispered back. "The World Cup in Mexico. That's when crowds all over the world saw it, so the name stuck in lots of countries." She pointed at the screen, where the wave was still rolling. "Folks in North America say the wave. Most everyone else says the Mexican wave."

So that was it. The wave had traveled out from Mexico in 1986, carrying Mexico's name with it, like a suitcase with a tag that never came off. Carson looked around the room. Nobody else had heard the exchange; they were all shouting at a corner kick. He thought about Jonah again, about how he had never asked where Jonah's grandpa's name for the fort came from, and how the fort was probably still standing there with the wrong name on it.

Only four minutes were left when the home team's striker broke free. Everyone in the living room stood up at once, and without planning it, arms lifted in order down the row, Mr. Okafor first, then Carson's dad, then Carson, then Priya. It rolled right past the window, where the wind spun the little turbine on the neighbor's roof, and Priya laughed and shouted over the roar, "Look, we made our own Mexican wave."

"Only if the whole world saw the 1986 World Cup first," Carson said, and Priya threw a popcorn kernel at him as the ball hit the net.

activity: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
knowledge_domain: to fast, pray or keep a day of rest for part of a day as their family does and explain why
fact: The Yom Kippur fast lasts about 25 hours, from sunset one day until after nightfall the next.
story:
Victor had eaten a big lunch on purpose, because tonight he was going to try the Yom Kippur fast for the first time, at Grandma Ruth's apartment with the whole family. He figured the hardest part would be missing dinner, so he had done the math in his head on the subway ride over: sunset was around six thirty, and sunset tomorrow was around six thirty, so twenty-four hours, no food, done. Twenty-four hours sounded hard but possible. Twenty-five would sound like something else entirely, though he had no reason to think about twenty-five yet.

"You're sure you want to do the whole thing?" Grandma asked, laying out the pre-fast meal of eggs and challah. "It's not mandatory for you until you're thirteen." Victor said he was sure, and Grandma didn't argue. She had compromised with him last month about Hebrew school, letting him skip one Sunday for a basketball tournament, and he suspected she was letting him win this one on purpose too. "Then eat well," she said, "because it's a long one."

The evening service was long, and the morning service was longer, and by noon Victor was lying on Grandma's couch with a growling stomach, counting hours on his fingers. He got to twenty-four around sunset and sat up, watching the window go orange and then gray. Six thirty came. Six forty-five came. "Grandma," he said, "the sun's down. Why aren't we eating?" She was still in her chair by the window, waiting, and she said, "We start after nightfall tomorrow, not at sunset. Sunset one day until after nightfall the next, about twenty-five hours in all." Victor flopped back against the cushion. He had fasted all this time believing he was on the last hour, and instead there was another one hiding past the sunset, an hour he couldn't see coming.

Later, after the stars came out and the family broke the fast with tea and honey cake, Victor found his grandfather in the kitchen, eating quietly by himself before everyone else. "You started before the blessing," Victor whispered. Grandpa shrugged. "1968. Hospital in Buffalo, Yom Kippur, my father sick. I told God I'd take one year off. Some years I pay it back, some years I don't." He held out a second fork. "You lasted twenty-five hours, Victor. Want to know the secret?" "What?" "The hour after is the best meal of the whole year," Grandpa said, and slid the cake closer.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel.
story:
Aaron wanted to win the craft competition at Camp Winnoway, and his plan was a spinning color wheel mounted on a little wooden propeller that would blur into white when he cranked it. The idea had come to him during movie night, when the projector flashed frames so fast the screen looked continuous. If fast frames could trick the eye, fast colors might too. He had painted red, orange, yellow, green, blue, and violet in a careful circle, each band touching the next in the same order they appeared in a rainbow.

The problem was the arrangement. His bunkmate Dex insisted that red belonged next to blue, because those were the colors of their rival camp, "united forever." Aaron said that seemed vague, like a rule somebody made up on the spot, but he could not prove which order was right. He decided to isolate the question. He cut two identical paper wheels, one with his rainbow order and one with Dex's, and he would spin both and compare.

Before he could test anything, mail call happened. Aaron got a postcard from his grandmother, who was staying in a cabin with no television. She wrote: "Dear Aaron, I found a paperback on a shelf here, all about the history of science. There is a fact in it you might like. In his book Opticks, first published in 1704, Isaac Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel. I thought of you because you never stop asking who thought of things first. Love, Grandma."

Aaron read it three times. "Dex," he said, holding up the postcard, "you're not going to believe this. Newton arranged the colors of the spectrum in a circle, an early form of the color wheel. In Opticks. First published in 1704. That's who thought of it first."

Dex squinted at the postcard. "Okay, fine," he said. "Red next to orange, then. Newton's order beats my order." He looked almost relieved. "Also I have been spelling your name wrong on my friendship bracelet, so I'm having a day of corrections."

They glued the wheels onto wooden propellers, stuck pins through the centers, and spun them hard between their palms. Newton's wheel blurred toward a pale gray. Dex's wheel, with red jammed against blue, blurred into a muddy streak that Dex described as "the color of lake socks." Aaron laughed so hard he dropped his pin in the sawdust.

At the competition, the judge cranked Aaron's wheel and watched it blur. "Who taught you this order?" she asked.

"Isaac Newton," Aaron said. "In a way."

"Newton, huh," said the judge, and spun it again.

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Coping means the ways a person handles stress or difficult feelings; healthy coping strategies include exercise, getting enough sleep and talking with someone trusted.
story:
The waiting room clock said 4:42, and a sign on the desk read "Last appointment 5:00," which gave Zoey eighteen minutes to figure out what she would actually say when the nurse called her name. Her stomach had hurt every morning for three weeks, and every afternoon it faded, like it was following some rule she couldn't see. Her mother flipped through a magazine. Zoey pulled out her phone under her jacket and opened a message from her best friend Priya.

"Bad day. Quiz bombed, then Leela kept grabbing my stuff and would not stop even when I asked. What do you do after a bad day? I need ideas."

Zoey thought about it while a poster on the wall showed a bee pollinating a purple flower, which had nothing to do with anything. She typed back: "I run around the block twice, even in rain. Then I sleep like a rock. Then I tell my mom everything." Priya answered fast: "I just scroll for hours and eat chips." Zoey hesitated, thumb hovering, then wrote: "That never makes mine better. Try the run and the sleep and the telling part." She added, "Also tell Leela your backpack is a boundary. Hands off." Priya sent back a bee emoji and the words "deal."

"Zoey?" the nurse called at 4:51, and Zoey's heart knocked against her ribs. In the exam room, the doctor asked questions, and when Zoey described the morning pain that vanished each afternoon, the doctor nodded slowly. "Any big changes at school lately?" Zoey thought of the tryout list that had gone up without her name on it, and of how she had told nobody.

"So what do you do to handle the stress?" the doctor asked.

"She runs, sleeps, and talks to me," her mother said.

"Those are healthy ones," the doctor said. "We call that coping."

The word landed in Zoey's mind and clicked into place like the last piece she'd been hunting for three weeks. Her stomach hurt on school mornings. It faded on weekends, which were all leisure and no tryout lists. The hidden cause had been sitting there the whole time, perpendicular to everything she'd blamed, like a line she'd never thought to draw.

"I know what it is," she said. "Can I text Priya? She'll never believe this."

activity: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
knowledge_domain: words such as anxiety, stress, coping and boundaries used to talk about mental health
fact: Feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when anxiety is intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, a doctor may diagnose an anxiety disorder, which is treatable.
story:
Alexa sat cross-legged on her bed with her notebook open and her door shut, which meant her brother had to knock before barging in. She wrote three words across the top of the page: stomache, sleep, school. For two weeks her stomach had knotted up like a wrung-out towel every morning, and last night she had lain awake until the ceiling turned gray with dawn. Was it the math test? The test was over now, but the knot was still there. That was the pattern she couldn't figure out. If the anxious feeling were only about the test, it should have vanished when the test did. Maybe she was missing the real cause, the way you miss a leak because the water shows up on a faraway ceiling.

She had budgeted her worry time like her dad budgeted money, giving herself ten minutes after dinner to feel anxious and then closing the drawer. It hadn't worked. The feeling leaked out anyway, into her intestine, her chest, her dreams about showing up to class with no shoes on. Her friend Priya knocked then, two soft raps, and Alexa waved her in.

"You look like you're doing a science experiment," Priya said, plopping onto the rug.

"Kind of. I'm trying to find the cause of my stomach knots. I ruled out the math test." Alexa turned the notebook so Priya could see.

Priya tilted her head. "Can I tell you something? Last year mine got so bad I couldn't eat lunch at school. It lasted months and it was messing up everything, so I told my mom, and she took me to a doctor. The doctor said feeling anxious sometimes is normal, but when it's really intense, lasts a long time and gets in the way of daily life, it can be an anxiety disorder. And that it's treatable." She shrugged. "It got better. Not like a trivial little thing you shake off, but actually better, because I got help."

Alexa stared at her list. So the problem might have a name, and a name might have a fix. She flipped to a clean page and wrote, "Tell Mom. Ask about doctor." Then she underlined it twice and slid the notebook across the rug.

"Can you come with me when I show her?"

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: If milk costs 2.65 and you pay with 5.00, the correct change is 2.35, whatever the currency.
story:
Samuel stood at the kitchen counter with five dollars in his hand and his mother's grocery list taped to his sleeve, which she said was for safety but mostly made him look like a walking receipt. "You're twelve now," she had said that morning. "You can supervise yourself at the corner store. Milk, whole, one gallon. Come straight back." Samuel had done the walk with her a hundred times, but alone felt different. Alone, the three blocks were full of dogs he had never noticed and cracks he had never counted.

Before he left, he did the math at the counter one more time, out loud, because his mother had taught him that saying numbers makes them stick. "Milk costs two sixty-five. I pay with five dollars. Five minus two sixty-five is two thirty-five." He tapped the bills against his palm. Two dollars and thirty-five cents was the exact change, no more and no less, and if the numbers on the shelf and the numbers in his hand stayed the same, the answer would stay the same too. It was almost like a law of the universe, and Samuel liked laws of the universe that fit in his pocket.

At the store, Mr. Delgado was on break and a teenage cashier with a name tag reading BRETT was running the register. Brett rang up the gallon, took Samuel's five dollars, and slid back two bills and a nickel. Samuel walked two steps toward the door, then stopped. He looked at the money in his hand. Two dollars and a nickel. He counted it again in his head, the way he had counted at the kitchen counter, and something did not fit.

He walked back to the register. "I think the change is wrong," he said, and his voice came out squeaky, which was not the plan. "The milk is two sixty-five and I paid with five, so the change should be two thirty-five." Brett squinted at the screen, then at the drawer, then said, "Oh. Dude. I gave you two oh-five." He dug into the register and added three dimes, sheepish as a cat who had been caught on the table. "Solid diagnosis, by the way. Most people just leave."

Samuel counted the full amount on the walk home, twice, and by the time he turned onto his own street he was grinning so hard that a neighbor's dog barked at him like he was up to something. In the kitchen his mother took the gallon and asked how it went.

"Made an influential purchase," Samuel said. "Brett respects me now."

"Who is Brett?"

Samuel set the change on the counter, every coin of the two thirty-five. "The cashier. He shorted me thirty cents, and I caught it."

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: A ranking shows order but not distance: first and second place might differ by a hundredth of a second or by a whole minute.
story:
Luca had watched the district swim finals on his cousin's phone four times already, and by the time the school bus rattled past the bakery on Miller Street, he was watching it a fifth. On the tiny screen, Rafael Deng touched the wall and threw his fists up. The silver medalist, a kid from Hollow Creek named Osei, had lost by four hundredths of a second. "Four hundredths," Luca muttered. "That's less than a blink."

Marcus slid into the seat across the aisle, crunching the brittle shell of a candy he'd smuggled out of last period. "You know who won, right? Rafael's ranked first in the whole league." He held up the sports app on his own phone. "Osei's ranked third. So Rafael's way better."

"Maybe," Luca said slowly. He didn't actually think maybe. He thought no, and it bothered him that he couldn't say why yet. Rankings were everywhere, on the app, on the news, even on the laminated list of cafeteria milk prices, and they all looked like they were telling you everything. First meant best. Third meant not as good. Case closed.

But the numbers on the race results page gave times, not just places, so Luca tried something. He wrote the top eight times on the back of his history worksheet, one under another, and subtracted each one from the next. First to second: four hundredths. Second to third: three hundredths. Then seventh to eighth, and his pencil stopped. The gap there was eleven whole seconds. He did it again in case he'd borrowed wrong. Eleven seconds. "Marcus," he said, "look at this. The ranking says they're all one step apart, but the steps aren't the same size. Rafael's first and Osei's second, and it's four hundredths. Seventh and eighth are a whole swim apart."

Marcus peered at the worksheet, chewing. "So the ranking is a lie?"

"It's not a lie, it's just..." Luca hunted for the word. "It shows who beat who. It doesn't show by how much. First and second could be four hundredths apart, or a whole minute apart, and the list looks exactly the same."

Marcus grinned and pulled out a crumpled paper from his backpack, the class ballot for team captain, still folded from lunch. "Okay, smart guy, then figure this out. The vote was me versus Dana, and I lost." He smoothed the ballot flat on his knee. "Does that mean Dana crushed me?"

Luca took the paper and counted the tallies under each name, his lips moving, the bus swaying around the corner by the gym. Then he started to laugh, and it took him a second to get the words out. "Marcus. It was fourteen to thirteen."

Marcus stared at the tally marks, then out the window, then back at the paper. "So technically," he said, "I lost by less than a blink." He held up his hand, and Luca high-fived it so hard the brittle candy crumbs jumped right off his worksheet.

activity: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
knowledge_domain: noticing the changes of growing up and puberty
fact: Hormones in puberty make oil glands in the skin produce more oil, called sebum, which can clog pores and lead to acne.
story:
The zit had appeared overnight, dead center on Emmett's chin, and school pictures were tomorrow morning at 8:40. He discovered it in the car's side mirror while his mom drove to Halsted's Pharmacy for toothpaste and laundry detergent. He leaned toward the glass, tilting his jaw. The bump was small but determined, like it had been appointed to its post specifically to ruin the photo.

"You've been staring at that mirror for three blocks," his mom said.

"I'm not staring." He turned forward. His little sister Ivy, mercifully absorbed in her tablet, didn't look up.

At the pharmacy, his mom headed for the detergent aisle, so Emmett drifted to the wall of face washes near the pharmacy counter. He had never once in his life looked at this shelf. There were at least thirty bottles, blue and orange and green, promising things like "oil control" and "deep clean." He picked one up, then another, comparing. The labels used the word "oil" over and over, but he didn't know why oil mattered. His face wasn't oily. It was just... broken out.

"Which one works?" said a voice. A girl from his grade, Priya, stood beside him holding two bottles, turning them over to read the backs.

"I have no idea," Emmett admitted. "I got a huge one on my chin and pictures are tomorrow."

"Same. Except mine are on my forehead." Priya held up a bottle. "Listen to this. It says it fights oil, so I looked up why. Puberty hormones make the oil glands in your skin produce more oil, and that oil is called sebum, and it clogs your pores and that's how you get acne. The whole thing is just plumbing."

Emmitt turned his own bottle over. "So the wash is trying to get the sebum out before it clogs anything."

"That's what I figured." Priya compared her two bottles again, squinting at the fine print. "This one says 'for oily skin' but doesn't actually say it removes oil. This one is explicit about it, right here: 'removes excess oil.' So this one."

He grabbed a matching bottle. Then he hesitated, because a thought had been building. "Wait. If hormones cause it, washing won't stop new oil from coming."

"Right, but it clears out what's there tonight." Priya shrugged. "It's the best we've got before 8:40 tomorrow."

His mom rounded the aisle with the detergent and gave the bottles a curious look. "New skincare routine?"

"Emergency," Emmett said.

At home, he washed his face exactly as the label directed, twice because he was nervous, and studied the chin in the bathroom mirror. The zit remained, slightly less angry, a small wave in what he suspected might turn out to be a tsunami. He set an alarm for 6:45 so he could wash again in the morning, and put the bottle on the sink where he couldn't miss it.

At breakfast, Ivy pointed at his chin. "What's that?"

"Sebum," Emmett said, and grabbed his backpack.

activity: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
knowledge_domain: to solve two-step equations and plot the line they describe on a coordinate grid
fact: In an ordered pair like (3, 5), the first number tells how far to move across along the x-axis and the second tells how far to move up or down.
story:
Michael had exactly four dollars and seventy-five cents, and the gumball machine at Nguyen's Corner Store held a red gumball that he wanted more than anything. The machine took only quarters, and the change machine by the register was broken, so he dumped his crumpled bills and random pennies onto the counter and started counting. Mr. Nguyen watched him sort, then slid a piece of graph paper across the counter.

"Your sister was in here yesterday," Mr. Nguyen said. "She left this." The paper had a coordinate grid on it, with a line drawn through some points, and at the top, in his sister Amy's handwriting: 2x + 3 = 9, and then (3, 5) circled twice.

Michael frowned. "That's my math homework," he said. "And her battleship game." Last night Amy had called (3, 5) on him, and he had insisted his ship was safe because he moved up five first and then across three. Amy had laughed so hard her milk almost came out her nose, and then she had refused to tell him why. She only said the answer was in the equation.

He counted his money again. Two quarters short. Mr. Nguyen was already ringing up a customer, so Michael sat on the crate by the ice cream freezer and stared at the paper. He tried the equation the way his teacher had started it in class. Something times two, plus three, makes nine. He thought about six, because six plus three was nine. Then the something had to be three, because three times two was six. So the line crossed x at three.

"So x is three," he muttered, and looked at the circled pair. Three had to be the first number. But which way did it go? He remembered Amy's battleship call, and her laughing. Maybe the first number was the across one, not the up one. He borrowed Mr. Nguyen's pencil and found 3 on the horizontal line at the bottom, moved across to it, then counted up five and marked a dot. Then he checked two more points from the grid, moving across by the first number and up by the second, and every single dot landed right on Amy's line. He tested it once more, carefully, in case the first try was just luck. The dots still landed on the line.

Michael grinned. He turned the paper over and wrote Amy a battleship challenge of his own, with coordinates all along the line. If she called (2, 7), she'd better mean across two first. Then he pushed the coins and bills across the counter. "Three dollars and seventy-five cents," he said, "and I'll sweep the floor for a dollar." Mr. Nguyen handed him a broom and, when the floor was done, two quarters.

At home, Michael held the gumballs in one hand and the paper in the other. He called out, "Amy! (1, 9)!" He heard a groan from behind the couch, then the sound of her battleship sinking.

activity: recovering from a cold or flu at home
knowledge_domain: recovering from a cold or flu at home
fact: A stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus.
story:
Jaxson sat at the kitchen table with a box of tissues, a trash can between his feet, and a nose that refused to cooperate. He blew for the ninth time that hour. Nothing came out, yet his nose still felt packed tight, like someone had stuffed a sock in each nostril.

"That's it," he said to his little sister, Priya, who was drawing a monarchy at the counter, a queen with a very tall crown and about forty pet hamsters. "I'm nominating chicken soup as the cure. Mom said it's in the freezer." He microwaved a bowl, ate it slowly, and waited. His throat felt better. His nose did not. He blew again, hard, and got almost nothing. "That doesn't make sense," he said. "If my nose is full of mucus, where is it? Why can't I blow it out?"

Priya looked up from her hamster palace. "Maybe it's not mucus." She had been home from school with the same cold last week, and she'd spent an entire afternoon on the couch with Mom's phone reading about it. "Mom read me that a stuffy nose during a cold is caused mainly by swollen blood vessels and inflamed tissue in the lining of the nose, not only by a buildup of mucus. Your nose is puffy inside. It's swollen shut."

Jaxson touched the side of his nose gently, thinking. If the blockage was swelling and not snot, then blowing harder was useless. Maybe even a bad idea. What helped swelling? He ran a towel under hot water, wrung it out, and held the warm cloth over his nose and cheeks like a bandit mask. Priya giggled. "You look like an impoverished robber." He breathed through the warmth, in and out, and slowly, the tightness loosened. Not gone, but looser.

"Okay," he said, setting down the tissues for good. "I'm done fighting a swamp that isn't even there." He slid the box across the table to Priya. "Keep these. Your turn is coming." Priya pointed her crayon at him and said, "Then you'll owe me a hot towel, bandit."

activity: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
knowledge_domain: to revise a draft by cutting weak adjectives and varying sentence length
fact: When every sentence is about the same length, writing tends to sound monotonous; mixing short and long sentences gives it rhythm.
story:
The story Kayla had written was called "The Race," and it was one hundred percent terrible, though she hadn't known that until her brother Dex read it aloud at the kitchen table while she ate her cereal.

"The morning was cool. The track was quiet. Maya was nervous. The other runners were fast. The race was about to begin." Dex paused. He read the next line. Then the next. By the fifth sentence his voice had gone flat as a pancake left out overnight, and by the tenth he was yawning into the page. "Sorry," he said. "It's just... nothing about it moves."

"You're the one who's not moving," Kayla said, but she took the draft back and stared at it. The dilemma was real. Ms. Reyes wanted a final copy tomorrow, and Kayla's problem wasn't that she had nothing to say. She had lots to say. It all just sat there.

She counted the words in each sentence. Four. Five. Four. Five. Six. Four. Every sentence was about the same length, like fence posts in a row. She wondered if that could be the trouble, though she couldn't see how sentence length would change anything on paper. It seemed logical, at least, to test it. She grabbed a pen.

First she cut the weak adjectives. "Cool morning" became "morning." "Fast runners" became just "the runners," because Maya could show they were fast by losing to them. Then she rebuilt the opening. She made one sentence long and winding, following Maya all the way from the parking lot to the starting line with her shoelaces double-knotted and her heart going like a drum. Then she made the next one very short.

"Nobody looked at her."

Dex glanced over from his toast. "Better," he said, which from Dex was practically a parade.

She kept going. Some sentences she stretched until they nearly snapped; others she chopped down to two or three words, and those little ones landed hard after the long ones, the way a single drop of water sounds loud after rain. She read a paragraph aloud to calibrate the effect, quietly at first, then in a full voice, because quiet wasn't telling her much. The rhythm was there. When every sentence had been about the same length, the story had sounded monotonous; mixed lengths gave it something like a pulse.

At the kitchen table the next morning, she slid the new draft across to Dex. He picked it up with the expression of a boy expecting to be bored.

"The gun went off. Maya ran."

He looked up. "Keep going," he said.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning is an ancient practice: the Book of Leviticus in the Hebrew Bible tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested for the poor and for strangers.
story:
Emily had been assigned to sort carrots at the food bank for two hours, and so far the carrots were winning. They came in boxes from a farm stand, and in every box, strange as it seemed, some carrots were wrapped separately in paper with a rubber band. Not the pretty ones. The crooked, split, ordinary ones.

At the third box she stopped and looked down the sorting table at Mr. Alvarez, whose granddaughter had dragged him along to volunteer. "Why would anyone wrap the ugly carrots?" she asked.

Mr. Alvarez squinted at one. "My grandmother used to do this. She called it gleaning."

"Gleaning?"

"From an old story. The Book of Leviticus, in the Hebrew Bible, tells farmers to leave the edges of their fields unharvested, for the poor and for strangers." He turned the carrot over like evidence. "No modern farm does that. But somebody here might."

So the wrapped carrots were not bizarre at all, Emily decided. They were the edges of the field. The question was who was leaving them, and why they never said so. She formed a verdict by the end of the hour: nobody at the food bank knew, because nobody at the food bank had ever asked.

She found her answer taped inside the fourth box, a folded note in pencil:

To whoever opens this. My father farmed forty acres and never once took the whole harvest. He said a field belongs partly to people you will never meet. I cannot farm, so I do this instead. Please do not tell anyone, it embarrasses my wife. Signed, a friend.

Emily read it twice, then went looking for Mr. Alvarez. He was in the back, excavating a pallet of dented cans that had slid half behind the shelving. She held out the note. He dried his hands on his jeans and read it, and then he laughed, quietly, the way you laugh at something that is not actually funny.

"That man," he said, "is doing a five-thousand-year-old thing with a rubber band."

Emily put the note back in the box, exactly where she had found it, and kept sorting. The next wrapped carrot she set down gently, like it was somebody's.

activity: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
knowledge_domain: to ask for directions in a new language and understand the answer
fact: In Mandarin Chinese, zuǒ means left and yòu means right, each said with its own tone.
story:
Raphael stood on Wei's front porch holding a folded map of the neighborhood, because Wei's grandmother had promised to walk them to the fruit market three blocks away, and Raphael had lost a bet that said he could get them there himself. The bet had gone badly at the first corner, where he turned them toward the school instead of the market, and Wei had laughed so hard he had to sit on a mailbox.

"You could just ask somebody," Wei said now, in a low voice, as his grandmother came out tying her sun hat.

"She doesn't speak much English," Raphael said. "Neither do the shop people."

"So learn two words," Wei said. "That's all it takes around here."

Grandma Chen patted the porch rail and said, "Zǒu ba," which Wei had told him once meant let's go. At the first intersection she stopped, held up her left hand, and said a word that dipped and fell, like someone sliding down a slide. "Zuǒ," she said, turning left. At the next corner she lifted her right hand and said a word that swooped down and then up, like a seagull. "Yòu." She did it again at every corner, left hand then right hand, the same two sounds each time, never mixed up.

Raphael kept his ears open and tested a small idea. The falling sound and the dipping sound were not the same word said two ways, they were two different words, and each one belonged to its own hand. He said "zuǒ" under his breath while raising his left hand, then "yòu" with his right, and Grandma Chen glanced back and smiled like he had passed some quiet quiz. Still, when he tried the right-hand word out loud at the next corner, the sound came out flat and wrong, and Wei's snort of laughter stung like a corrosive splash, eating at his pride a little. He thought about the bet, about how he had refused to ask the crossing guard for directions last Saturday because it felt like admitting weakness. Maybe that choice had cost him more than the nickel he owed.

Grandma Chen stopped in front of a door with red lanterns and said a long sentence Raphael could not follow, but he caught one word in it, yòu, and she pointed to the right side of the market entrance, where a stall sold roasted chestnuts. He realized she had disclosed the answer to a question he hadn't even known how to ask: the chestnuts were on the right.

"Zǒu zuǒ?" he tried inside the market, lifting his left hand toward the fruit aisle.

"Zuǒ," Grandma Chen agreed, and steered him left with two fingers on his shoulder. He would practice the swoop of yòu later, on the walk home, and next time he would ask before he lost the nickel.

"Pick the big ones," Wei said, holding up a pear. "Yòu side of the bin."

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Psychologist Lee Ross named the fundamental attribution error in 1977: the tendency to blame others' actions on their personality while underestimating their situation.
story:
Marcus had been at Dev's house for exactly eleven minutes when Maya stormed through the kitchen and slammed her mug down so hard that coffee slopped across the counter. "Some people have no respect," she snapped, without looking at either of them, and then she was gone, her bedroom door booming shut behind her. Dev winced and kept arranging the ant farm on the table. "That's my sister," he said. "She's like that."

Marcus wasn't so sure. Maya had driven them to the pool last weekend and had been funny the whole way there, joking about the geese that seemed determined to colonize the whole parking lot. A person didn't just turn into a slamming-doors person overnight, did it? But maybe she did. Maybe the pool trip had been a one-time fluke and the real Maya was the mug-slamming Maya. He wanted to know, because if Maya was truly mean, he'd rather know before he asked her the big favor: she owned the only real microscope in the neighborhood, and Dev had promised they could look at the ants up close.

While Dev searched the garage for tweezers, Marcus noticed things. Maya's phone lay on the counter, screen lit up, buzzing again and again. There were missed calls, a dozen of them, all from somebody labeled Nonna. Her chair was pushed back from the table at an odd angle, like she'd jumped up mid-meal. And her coffee wasn't even coffee; it was cocoa, half untouched, which was strange for a girl who bragged about drinking three espressos a day. Maybe the slam wasn't about personality. Maybe it was about whatever was on that phone.

Then he heard her voice through the wall, thin and wobbly, the way his own voice had gone when their dog ran off last spring. "Is she okay? Tell me she's okay." Marcus stood very still. He couldn't see her, and he couldn't see what the calls were about, but he could see the shape of it now, the way you can guess at a rule after watching enough examples.

On the counter, Dev's little speaker was still playing the podcast his dad had left on. The voice was saying, "In 1977, psychologist Lee Ross named it the fundamental attribution error: we blame other people's actions on their personality while underestimating their situation." Marcus nudged Dev. "The fundamental attribution error," he whispered. "That's what I just did to your sister." Dev nodded slowly, then pointed at the hallway, where Maya was coming out with red eyes and her car keys. "Hospital bag's in the trunk," she said. "Nonna fell. You two okay here?" Marcus held up the ant farm. "Can we look at them under your microscope when you get back?" Maya managed half a smile. "If you wash my mug."

activity: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
knowledge_domain: to find the theme of a novel and back it up with a quotation from the text
fact: In MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks.
story:
Autumn clutched her copy of "The War That Saved My Life" so hard the paperback cover bent. Six kids sat in Mrs. Alvarez's library corner, the book club's final meeting of the semester, and each of them had to name the theme and back it up with a quotation. Ben went first, saying the theme was courage, and read a short line from page 112. Easy. Autumn's theme was conscience, the voice inside that tells you right from wrong, but her favorite passage was long, and she had copied all of it onto an index card because she could not bear to cut it.

She remembered the night she found it, sitting on her bed with hot chocolate gone cold and a waxy chocolate smell still on her fingers, reading the scene where Jamie admits what he did with the iron. She had underlined it three times. It was the most eloquent thing in the whole book, and now she would have to chop it up like a carrot.

When her turn came, she tried anyway. "The theme is conscience," she said, "because Ada realizes that, quote, knowing what's right is," she flipped the card, "quote, not the same as," flip, "doing it, unquote." Everyone blinked. Priya started giggling, then covered her mouth. "You said quote four times," Ben said. "It's like a sandwich inside a sandwich."

Autumn frowned at the card, which was eight lines long. Then she remembered the packet Mrs. Alvarez had left on the table, the one she had stuffed in her bag last week and forgotten. She dug it out, and there it was, plain on the page: in MLA style, a prose quotation longer than four lines is set as an indented block, half an inch from the margin, without quotation marks. Her passage was eight lines, so no quotation marks at all. She would not have to swallow it into one sentence.

She pulled a fresh sheet from her binder, indented the whole passage half an inch with her thumb on the ruler edge, and wrote it out clean. "It's a block," she said, standing up. "Listen." Then she read Ada's words to the whole circle, straight through, without one single quote.

activity: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
knowledge_domain: to use loops and if-then blocks in Scratch to make a game that keeps score
fact: In Scratch, a 'repeat 10' block runs the blocks inside it exactly ten times, while a 'forever' block keeps going until the program is stopped.
story:
Zoey had been building her game all afternoon, and tonight she planned to show it to her cousin Marco over video chat. The idea was simple: an army of green cats would invade the screen, and the player, a tiny mouse with a sword, had to tag them before they reached the cheese. Every tag was worth a point, and the score climbed at the top of the screen like a leaderboard at a bowling alley.

There was only one problem, and it was a strange one. When she clicked the green flag, the cats marched toward the cheese, moving one step at a time, and then they just stopped. All of them. Every single cat froze in place halfway across the screen and stood there looking lethargic, like they had decided to take a collective nap. The mouse could still tag them, and the score still worked, but a game where the invaders give up on invading was not much of a game at all.

She leaned close to the screen. The cats weren't crashing into anything. There was no wall, no edge, nothing blocking them. Something invisible was stopping them, and she meant to find it. She zoomed in on one cat's code and read it block by block, like taking a census of every piece until she counted them all. Under the green flag sat a stack with the words "repeat 10" wrapped around a single block that said "move 10 steps."

"Move ten steps, ten times," she said slowly. She did the math on her fingers. That was how far the cats had gotten, and then no farther. She deleted the repeat block and dragged over a different one, a thick orange one that wrapped all the way around her move block. "Forever," she read aloud.

Marco's call came through right as she clicked the flag. The cats surged toward the cheese, and none of them stopped. The mouse scrambled, tagging wildly, and the score spun upward.

"Whoa," Marco said. "They're relentless."

"Forever," Zoey said, and tagged two more.

activity: trying out for a school sports team
knowledge_domain: trying out for a school sports team
fact: Studies of youth sports have found that players born early in the selection year are picked for teams more often than those born late, which researchers call the relative age effect.
story:
Raphael taped the cut list to the refrigerator, which his mother said was a strange thing to do with bad news. He had a reason, though. He wanted to look at it while he ate his cereal every morning until it stopped stinging, the way you keep touching a sore tooth.

His little sister Priya wandered in with her own agenda. "Is the kitchen table free tonight? I need it for my volcano."

"The volcano exploded already. Twice."

"It needs a rebuild. Mine has to be the most eloquent one in the class. Mrs. Teller gives extra credit for presentations that seem like real lava." Priya wanted that extra credit the way Raphael had wanted the team, so he shoved the cut list over and made room.

At school he found Dev, who had made the team, in the hallway by the gym. "Can I see the roster? The posted one with everybody's names?"

"You want to torture yourself?"

"Just curious."

Dev peeled the sheet off the cork board and handed it over. Raphael copied the birthdays into his notebook while sweat made the pages damp and he tried not to perspire onto the ink. Out of fifteen names, eleven had birthdays in the first half of the year. Dev himself was February. Four had the second half. Only one boy, a January kid, had been cut, and only two late-year kids had made it. Raphael was December. Youngest possible kid in the whole grade, by the calendar the school used for sorting players.

He showed Dev the notebook. "Look at the pattern."

"That's a coincidence," Dev said, and then, squinting, "maybe."

Raphael looked it up that night on the family computer, keyboard still gritty with Priya's volcano clay. There it was, plain as a bus schedule: studies of youth sports had found that players born early in the selection year were picked for teams more often than those born late.

"What's that called?" Priya asked, leaning over his shoulder like a small curious organism drawn to a light.

"The relative age effect," Raphael read aloud.

"Huh. So what are you going to do?"

"Try out again next year. And this year, I'm going to get so good they can't cut me no matter what month I was born in." He stood up, went to the garage, and pulled his basketball off the shelf.

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Watering deeply and less often encourages roots to grow downward, while frequent light sprinkling keeps roots near the surface where soil dries fastest.
story:
Ellie split her garden into two square plots behind the barn, one for tomatoes and one for carrots, and wrote the plan on a popsicle stick. She would sprinkle the first plot lightly every single evening, because that felt like giving the plants a drink every day, and she would soak the second plot only twice a week, until the ground went dark and soft all the way down. Her little brother Owen had his own want: a stand at the end of the driveway by July, selling vegetables for money toward a new bike bell. "We have to classify what we grow," he announced, holding up a marker. "Tomatoes, fruit or vegetable? Customers will ask."

For three weeks both plots looked fine. Ellie hauled water from the hand pump, whose handle rose and fell like a piston while she counted out twenty slow strokes for the deep plot and five quick ones for the sprinkled plot. Owen stayed busy guarding the tomato side from the barn cat, a predatory orange thing that liked to flatten herself in the young rows and swat at leaves.

Then the hot week came. Five days of sun with no rain, and Ellie woke on the sixth morning to find the sprinkled plot drooping hard, leaves folded over like closed umbrellas, while the deep-watered plot stood green and almost cheerful beside it. She knelt and pressed her finger into each plot's soil. The sprinkled side was bone dry at the top. The deep side still held dampness down where her finger reached.

"Same sun," she said slowly. "Same everything. Except the water." She pulled up one wilted carrot seedling from the sprinkled plot, then dug carefully around one from the deep plot, and laid them side by side on the porch step. The wilted one's roots were short, huddled near the surface. The other one's roots ran down, long and pale, deeper than she expected.

Owen crouched beside her. "So light watering every day kept the roots up top," he said, "and deep watering once in a while made them grow down." He pointed at the dried crust of soil. "And the top dries out fastest, so up top is the worst place to be."

"Exactly," Ellie said. She grabbed the watering can and headed for the drooping plot. "New rule. We soak this one deep, twice a week, starting now."

Owen grabbed the second can and ran to catch up, marker still behind his ear. "My bell is going to be the loudest one on the street," he called, and poured.

activity: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
knowledge_domain: to walk to the corner store alone, buy milk and count the change
fact: In the United States and Canada, shelf prices usually leave out sales tax, which is added at the till; in the UK and EU, shown prices already include VAT.
story:
Everly folded her list one more time and squinted at the doors of the driving school. The sign said RIDGEVIEW INDEPENDENCE DRIVING SCHOOL, and underneath, in smaller letters, "Where you learn to drive your own life." That was Mr. Okonkwo's joke on the first day, and Everly still thought it was funny, even though her older brother groaned every time she repeated it. Today was the last class before the real test: walk to Herrera's corner store alone, buy one carton of milk, and count the change correctly.

"Last week we transmitted the route into our feet," Mr. Okonkwo said, clapping his hands. "Two blocks, cross at the light with the chirping signal, store on the right. Who is today's candidate?" Everly's hand shot up before she could talk herself out of it. Her cousin Freya had done this walk alone in London last summer, and Freya was a year younger. Everly wanted her turn.

She set out with eleven coins zipped in her front pocket, counted three times at the kitchen table this morning. At Herrera's she found the milk herself, checked the tag on the shelf, and read it twice: two dollars and forty-nine cents. She carried it to the counter, laid out exactly that much, and slid it toward Mr. Herrera, who was already scanning the carton while his radio murmured behind him.

The register beeped and showed two dollars and sixty-six cents. Everly stared at it, then at her empty palm. Seventeen cents short, and she had counted perfectly, she knew she had. "That can't be right," she said. "The shelf says two forty-nine." Mr. Herrera tapped the screen. "Shelf price here doesn't include sales tax. Tax gets added at the till." Everly's face went warm. Then she remembered Freya complaining on the phone last summer, saying shops in the UK were easier because the price on the shelf already included VAT, so you never had to do math in your head. Freya had said her friend in Paris paid the shelf price too, because it worked the same way in the EU. Here, the number on the tag was only part of the number at the register.

She tested it right there, because she wanted to be sure it was a rule and not a mistake. "So the cereal that says four dollars is really more than four dollars?" Mr. Herrera nodded. "Every time." Behind her, a boy about her age was jingling a handful of coins, looking worriedly at a candy bar. Everly turned and counted what he held. "You're short too," she said. "You need a bit more than the sticker says." The boy sighed and swapped the candy bar for a smaller one, and Everly paid her milk in full with a quarter Mr. Herrera lent her, promising to bring it back next week.

She walked out into the afternoon light, which had turned molten gold on the parked cars along the curb. In her pocket, the change jingled: one dime, one nickel, one penny, and two pennies she would return with the quarter. She counted them again at the corner, waiting for the chirp, and grinned at the crosswalk like it was a finish line. "I drove," she said out loud, and stepped off the curb.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: In a physical change, a substance changes its shape or state but stays the same substance, the way ice melting into water is still water.
story:
Hazel pressed her nose against the glass case in the museum's Matter Room, where a bowl of ice cubes sat under a warm lamp, slowly turning to puddle. Her best friend Dexter stood beside her, clutching his quiz card like it was a golden ticket.

"If I get all five questions right, I win a glow-in-the-dark dinosaur sticker," Dexter said. "Question three is the tricky one. Was anything new made when the ice melted?"

Hazel frowned at the puddle. "New made? It's just... wet now."

"That's not an answer. That's a shrug with words."

Behind them, an old volunteer named Mr. Okafor wheeled in a cart of exhibits from the museum's most dilapidated wing, the one with the squeaky door and the flickering lights. On the cart sat a rusty horseshoe, a burnt match, and a photograph of the tundra, frozen ground that never thaws all the way. He parked the cart and wandered off to find his reading glasses.

Hazel stared at the rusty horseshoe. It was orange and flaky, nothing like shiny silver metal. The burnt match was black crumbly ash. Then she looked back at the puddle. She dipped her finger in the meltwater and touched it to her tongue. Plain water. Cold, plain water.

"Dexter," she said slowly, "the ice was water, and now it's water again. It only changed shape, like squishing clay. It's still the same substance. But that horseshoe rusted, and the match burned, and those are different stuff now, stuff that wasn't there before."

Dexter scribbled on his card. "So melting is a physical change," he read off the card, "and rusting and burning are chemical changes. Wait, how do you know these words?"

"Read them off the horseshoe label while you were showing off your sticker card."

Dexter wrote his answer, marched to the front desk, and came back holding the sticker high. Then he slapped it on Hazel's shirt.

"For the taste test," he said. "Bravest tongue in the museum."

Hazel grinned and peeled it off, sticking it on the glass right beside the melting ice.

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Burning is a chemical change: wood combines with oxygen and turns into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour, and it cannot turn back into wood.
story:
The letter from Mason's grandfather had been sitting in his backpack since morning, and he read it again at lunch instead of eating his apple. "The ice fishing shack burned down last week," it said. "Frosty was upset because he'd left a cooler of ice in there and it melted everywhere, but I told him the ice was the least of it. Come up this weekend and we'll build a new one. Bring your science brain." Mason folded the letter and looked at the apple, then at the brown edge where it had gone soft. His friend Priya slid her tray across from him, but she wasn't looking at him. She was looking at the science fair sign-up sheet in her hand.

"I need a partner for the demonstration table," she said. "Mrs. Okafor picked me to run it, and if nobody signs up, I have to do it alone in front of the whole sixth grade." Priya wanted one thing in this world, and that was to be in charge of something. Mason said yes before he'd finished chewing, mostly because he'd been wondering all day about the shack. Something bothered him. Frosty's ice had melted, and the shack had burned, and those felt like the same kind of accident, except they weren't. He could say why the ice wasn't the problem, but not why the fire was.

In the lab after school, Mrs. Okafor had set out a tray with an ice cube, a steel nail in a jar of damp air, and a small piece of charcoal in a dish. She said only, "Show the visitors the difference," and left them to it. Priya held up the ice cube as it dripped onto the tray. "Easy. This melts and you can freeze it back. Same stuff, just warmer." She set it down and frowned at the charcoal. "Now what do we say about this?"

Mason turned the charcoal over with tongs. His grandfather's letter had said the shack burned down, and nobody ever said a burned shack came back. He said, slowly, trying the idea out loud, "When it burns, the wood isn't just warmer. It's combining with oxygen. It turns into ash, carbon dioxide and water vapour." He picked up the ash tray. "This can't turn back into wood. It's a chemical change." Priya wrote it on an index card, then tested him on it twice, because she was in charge.

At home, Mason carried his apple core to the back step and watched the brown spread across it. He was still turning things over in his mind the next morning when he helped his father load the truck to transport firewood up to the property for the new shack. "Don't be like Frosty," his father said, stacking the last logs. "He's full of resentment about that cooler. Says Gramps should transport the ice in a thermos next time." Mason laughed, then thought of the pile of ash waiting up north, and of the nutritious soup his grandfather would make from whatever hadn't burned, and of Frosty insisting the ice was the real loss.

"Grandpa," Mason said when they arrived Saturday, holding up the index card Priya had made him memorize, "Frosty's ice could freeze back. The wood can't."

Frosty squinted at him from a folding chair. "It's just wood."

"It's not," Mason said. "It went into the sky."

activity: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
knowledge_domain: to draw a food chain from the sun to a top predator and explain what happens when one link disappears
fact: Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest.
story:
Emily sat on the farmhouse porch with her notebook open to a blank page, because her teacher had assigned a food chain starting with the sun and ending with a top predator, and Emily wanted hers to be the one pinned to the classroom wall. She knew the farm well enough: grass in the pasture, grasshoppers in the grass, frogs by the creek, and a pair of hawks that circled the big oak every afternoon. She drew arrows from the sun to the grass to the grasshoppers to the frogs to the hawks, then frowned. The assignment had a second part, explain what happens when one link disappears, and she could not picture it.

Then she remembered the science museum last summer, where her cousin Daniel had built a block arch and pulled out the single top middle stone. The whole arch had collapsed. A guide had told them the same idea existed in nature, and Emily, trying to formulate the question she wanted to ask, had blurted out, "You mean like one animal matters more than the others?" The guide had said, "Robert Paine introduced the term 'keystone species' in 1969 for a species whose removal changes its whole community far more than its numbers would suggest." Emily had written the words on the back of her museum ticket.

She dug the crumpled ticket out of her jacket pocket. On the back, in her own handwriting, was the guide's line, and below it a note she had sent herself: check if frogs count. She ran down to the creek and spent an hour counting, keeping her tally objective, marking down what she saw rather than what she hoped for. Frogs were a small percentage of the animals in the pasture, but when she imagined the creek going quiet, she could see the grasshoppers multiplying and the hawks hunting harder and everything shifting.

Her grandmother called from the porch, "Supper in ten minutes." Emily shaded the frog link dark and wrote one word beside it, then held the notebook up so the late sun lit the page. "Keystone," she said.

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: Psychologists distinguish forgiving, which means letting go of resentment, from reconciling, which means rebuilding the relationship; a person can forgive someone without the friendship returning to exactly how it was.
story:
Rebecca sat at the kitchen counter with the family group chat open on her mom's phone, since her own was confiscated for the week. The chat had 23 unread messages, most of them from her little brother Marcus, who was campaigning to be allowed more screen time if he complied with every chore on the fridge list. Rebecca scrolled past all of it, looking for one thing: whether her mom had answered her private question from last night. She had typed it at eleven p.m., which she knew was risky. The question said, "Is it possible to forgive Priya but not want to be best friends again yet, or is that cheating?" Priya had blurted out Rebecca's secret in front of the whole lunch table on Tuesday, and the two of them had not spoken since.

Her mom's reply was waiting. "Forgiving means letting go of the resentment. Reconciling means rebuilding the relationship. They are two different things. You can do one without the other. Forgiving Priya does not have to mean the friendship goes back to exactly how it was." Rebecca read it three times. She had assumed forgiving someone meant pretending nothing happened, an all-or-nothing alloy of sorry and back to normal, fused together. The idea that the two could come apart felt strange, then possible, then like a door she could actually walk through.

She typed a reply with her thumbs while Marcus peered over her shoulder. "Can you text Priya's mom and ask if Priya can meet me at the park at four? Also Marcus gets his screen time, he did every chore, I checked." Marcus whooped and ran for the fridge list to prove it.

At the park, Priya was already on the swing, dragging her sneakers in the wood chips. "I'm sorry," Priya said before Rebecca even sat down. "I wasn't trying to be mean, it just came out." Rebecca took the swing beside her. "I forgive you. But I'm not ready for sleepovers yet. Is that allowed?" Priya thought about it, then pushed off with both feet. "Yeah. Race you to the fence."

activity: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
knowledge_domain: to tell a physical change like melting from a chemical change like rusting or burning
fact: Dissolving salt in water is a physical change, because evaporating the water leaves the same salt behind.
story:
On Tuesday the science lab smelled like vinegar, which Jessica found impressive, since the lesson was on chemical changes and Mr. Duffy had only written one word on the board. That word was CHANGE, underlined twice, as if the underline would preserve its meaning. Her lab partner, Marcus, had already knocked over a beaker by reflex, before anything had even happened to react to. "Rusting is chemical," Jessica muttered, copying the chart. "Burning is chemical. Melting is just... physical. The stuff is still the stuff."

The problem was the last row of the chart, the one Mr. Duffy had left blank on purpose. Dissolving salt in water: physical or chemical? Marcus shrugged with his whole body. Jessica held the beaker up to the light and watched the grains vanish, which felt like the salt was gone forever, destroyed, turned into something new. But something about that bothered her. "When ice melts, it's still water," she said. "If I evaporated this water, would the salt come back?"

She didn't wait for permission. She poured a shallow layer of the salt solution into a petri dish, wrote her name on tape with the extravagant flourish of someone making history, and set it on the sunny windowsill behind the fern. Then she waited, which turned out to be the hardest part of any experiment ever conducted. Wednesday: still wet. Thursday: less wet. Marcus checked it more often than she did, hovering like the dish owed him money.

Friday morning, the dish was dry. Around the edges sat a crust of tiny white crystals, sharp and glittery, and in the middle a scattering of small square shapes that had not been there before. Jessica touched one with a fingertip and tasted it before she could talk herself out of that. Salt. The exact same salt. She carried the dish to Marcus and held it out. "It's a physical change," she announced. "The water left and took nothing with it." Mr. Duffy leaned over from the next table, peered into the dish, and gave her a thumbs-up with a hand still holding somebody's rusty nail.

activity: watching a big game with family and friends
knowledge_domain: watching a big game with family and friends
fact: James Naismith invented basketball in December 1891 at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts, using peach baskets as the goals.
story:
The Hendersons' basement smelled like popcorn and damp coats, because the whole neighborhood had squeezed in to watch the championship game on their giant television. Carter had the best spot, right in front on the carpet, next to Mr. Henderson's humming generator, which kept the TV running whenever the storm outside knocked the power out. Rain tapped the high window, and the room felt humid with so many people cheering and groaning in one small space.

During a timeout, Carter's little sister Priya frowned at the screen. "Why do they even call it a basket? Nobody's carrying a basket. It's a net with a hole in the bottom."

Half the room started guessing at once. Uncle Ray said it was just an old word that stuck. Priya's friend Marta suggested it came from the shape. Their answers contradicted each other, so Carter knew at least some of them were wrong, and probably all of them. He wanted the real answer before the game ended, because Priya asked questions like a dog with a bone and would not let it go.

The clock showed eight minutes left in the second half. Carter went upstairs to the kitchen, where Mrs. Henderson kept a shelf of old books. He had seen a dusty blue one up there last summer, something about sports history. He found it wedged between a cookbook and a phone book, flipped through the thin pages, and there it was, with an old black-and-white photograph of men in a gymnasium.

"Listen," Carter said, sliding back down the stairs just as the third quarter buzzer sounded. "Basket was invented in December of 1891 by a man named James Naismith. He made it up at a YMCA training school in Springfield, Massachusetts." Priya asked what the goals were, and Carter pointed at the picture. "Peach baskets. They nailed peach baskets up as the goals. That's why it's called a basket."

"Peach baskets," Priya repeated, satisfied, and settled back against the couch.

The lights flickered once, twice, and everyone held their breath, but the generator hummed steadily on and the screen stayed bright. With four seconds left, the home team's guard launched a shot from way outside. It dropped through the net without touching the rim, and the whole humid basement erupted. Carter stood up with the book still under his arm, grinning at the television.

"Somewhere," he told Priya over the shouting, "that went in a peach basket."

activity: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
knowledge_domain: to add and subtract fractions with unlike denominators by finding a common denominator
fact: Multiplying two denominators together always gives a common denominator, though it is not always the smallest one.
story:
The clock above the whiteboard gave Colton nine minutes, and the math club trophy was on the line. Mrs. Ruiz had taped a puzzle to each table, and the first pair to solve every problem would represent the school at the county meet.

"You do the fractions," Priya whispered, sliding the paper toward him. "I'll take the geometry."

Colton stared at the first problem: three fourths plus one sixth. Fourth graders could add fractions. He had watched them do it. But their fractions had matching bottoms, like two puzzle pieces from the same box. These two did not match at all.

He thought back to October, to the morning his grandfather had rebuilt the porch steps. Two boards of different widths, six inches and nine. Grandpa had lined them up, marked, sawn, and suddenly both were twelve inches wide. "Same size," he had said, "or you can't build anything straight." Colton had thought that was only about wood.

He gripped his pencil. The bottoms were four and six. They didn't match, so he couldn't just add the tops. What if he made them match, like the boards?

Four times six is twenty-four, he wrote. He multiplied the top of the first fraction by six and the top of the second by four, and both fractions now sat over twenty-four. Eighteen twenty-fourths plus four twenty-fourths equaled twenty-two twenty-fourths. He checked it twice. It had to be right.

Priya leaned over. "The answer key says eleven twelfths."

Colton's stomach dropped. Eleven twelfths. He looked at his twenty-two twenty-fourths and felt his face go hot. Then he divided top and bottom by two, and there it was: eleven twelfths. His answer had been right, only fatter, like a suitcase packed for the tundra when a backpack would do. He raised his hand anyway.

"My answer's bigger than yours," he told Mrs. Ruiz, showing both papers, "but it's the same amount."

Mrs. Ruiz smiled. "Multiplying the denominators together always gives you a common denominator. It just isn't always the smallest one."

"Like Grandpa's boards," Colton said, mostly to himself. "It still fits, it's just more cutting." He wrote the next problem, one third plus two fifths, and beneath it, fifteen. Somewhere behind him, another table scratched furiously at their paper.

"Six minutes," Priya hissed.

Colton put his pencil down and started to add.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
Declan had inherited his grandfather's heavy copper saucepan, and he intended to use it tonight to make caramel sauce for the vanilla ice cream waiting in Grandma's freezer. He had one problem: the last time he'd tried, at home, the sugar had gone from pale gold to black and bitter in what seemed like two seconds. Here at his grandparents' house, on a stove he didn't know, he had to figure out what he couldn't see directly, the exact moment the browning was done, before the pan told him by ruining it.
